tldr: By combining high-level natural language coordination via VLMs with low-level fine-grained control via VLAs, this work achieves distributed multi-robot collaborative manipulation without relying on centralized control, leveraging the strengths of large-scale foundation models.

(b) Overview of RoboPoly, the long-horizon coordination benchmark introduced in this work. (c) Task success rates improve substantially compared to standalone end-to-end foundation models.
overview:
Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have rapidly improved single robots' ability to follow instructions and execute flexible behaviors. However, in real-world scenarios with complex workflows and expansive workspaces, multi-robot coordination is essential. Prior work has largely focused on single robots or centralized systems controlling two arms with a single brain. In a truly distributed setting—where each robot operates with its own field of view and independent compute—preventing collisions while efficiently dividing labor remains exceptionally difficult.

To tackle this, the authors introduce "DuoMind," a distributed hierarchical framework for multi-robot coordination. The core idea is very smart: each robot is equipped with a "thinking brain" (a VLM) and an "acting brain" (a VLA). The VLMs exchange semantic messages in natural language, sharing statements such as "I am going to do this" or "The tray is over there." This setup enables robots to share intentions and avoid collisions while directly reusing powerful existing single-robot foundation models.

The authors also developed "RoboPoly," a long-horizon manipulation benchmark requiring tight physical coordination under distributed control, and evaluated DuoMind alongside the existing "RoboTwin" benchmark. DuoMind achieved significantly higher success rates than traditional standalone VLA baselines. Furthermore, cutting off inter-robot communication caused frequent collisions and deadlocks, vividly illustrating that natural language intent-sharing is indispensable for multi-robot coordination.
contributions: Proposed DuoMind, a distributed multi-robot coordination framework hierarchically combining global reasoning and communication via VLMs with local control via VLAs.

Enabled collision-free collaborative manipulation under partial observability by exchanging structured natural language messages among agents containing intentions, subgoals, beliefs, and uncertainties.

Built and released RoboPoly, a long-horizon bimanual and multi-robot manipulation benchmark requiring distributed observations and physical collaboration, along with a high-quality demonstration dataset.

Demonstrated substantial improvements in task success rates over standalone foundation model baselines (π0, π0.5) on both RoboPoly and RoboTwin, quantitatively validating the benefits of semantic communication and hierarchical orchestration through ablations.

sections.heading: Why Pursue Distributed Multi-Robot Coordination with Language Models Now?
sections.summary: While single-robot VLA models have progressed rapidly, distributed multi-robot coordination remains challenging yet crucial for real-world deployment. To bridge the gap between high-level language reasoning and low-level motor control, this work proposes DuoMind featuring a hierarchical structure and semantic communication, alongside the new benchmark RoboPoly.
sections.details:
The emergence of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) capable of visual reasoning and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models capable of directly outputting robot actions has fueled rapid progress in general-purpose robotics. However, most research remains confined to single-robot scenarios. Real-world tasks frequently require collaboration that exceeds the capacity of a single robot, such as transporting items beyond reach or cooperatively carrying heavy objects.

When coordinating multiple robots, distributed execution—where each robot makes decisions locally based on its own camera inputs—offers far superior scalability compared to centralized control managed by a single monolithic computer. However, achieving fine-grained motor control while predicting the partner's actions under partial observability (where each robot cannot see the other's wrist camera and views only a portion of the workspace) is exceptionally challenging.

Most existing multi-agent studies using LLMs rely on abstract symbolic planning or calling predefined primitive skills, leaving a significant disconnect from end-to-end closed-loop control. Furthermore, benchmarks to properly evaluate long-horizon physical tasks in distributed multi-robot setups have been lacking. To address these gaps, this work introduces DuoMind, placing a pretrained VLM as an orchestrator and a VLA as an action model on each robot, linked together via natural language communication.

sections.heading: How DuoMind Works: A Hierarchical Architecture Centered on Natural Language
sections.summary: By equipping each robot with a VLM orchestrator and a VLA action model, low-frequency high-level reasoning is decoupled from high-frequency low-level control. Robots communicate using structured natural language messages that convey intent and perception, preventing collisions and deadlocks under partial observability.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Multi-Agent Coordination via Embodied Reasoning
The defining feature of DuoMind is clearly separating complex multi-robot coordination into two tiers: high-level reasoning/communication and low-level precise control. Training a VLA directly on multi-view inputs from multiple robots to handle coordination requires massive amounts of training data, primarily because existing VLAs are pretrained on single-arm datasets. In DuoMind, each robot's VLM digests environmental cues and incoming peer messages, breaking them down into short single-arm subgoals (such as "grasp the bread and place it in the center") for the local VLA. This allows existing single-robot foundation models to be utilized almost out of the box.

### 2.2 Hierarchical Coupling and Communication via Natural Language
Natural language serves as the communication interface connecting the high-level VLM to the low-level VLA. Compared to trajectory or latent vector interfaces, natural language offers outstanding modularity: when stronger VLMs or VLAs become available in the future, components can be upgraded simply by swapping them in. Additionally, natural language acts as a universal protocol when coordinating heterogeneous robots from different manufacturers or allowing human operators to intervene.

### 2.3 Structured Message Exchange Between Agents
In distributed environments, agents can easily miss what their peers are doing. To solve this, DuoMind's VLM orchestrators exchange structured text messages containing four key fields:
- **Intention**: The subtask description that the robot will execute via its VLA next. This informs the peer robot in advance, avoiding spatial conflicts.
- **Subgoals**: The expected state upon subtask completion, allowing the partner robot to proactively initiate complementary actions.
- **Belief of task**: Local environment information observed by the robot's camera (e.g., "the pot is on the third shelf") shared with the partner.
- **Uncertainty of belief**: A confidence signal reflecting how certain the robot is about its reasoning, preventing erroneous decisions based on ambiguous visual inputs.

The high-level VLM orchestrator reasons at a lower frequency to generate short natural language instructions for the low-level VLA action model, while simultaneously exchanging structured messages with the peer robot to coordinate intentions.

sections.heading: RoboPoly Benchmark: Realistic, Distributed, and Long-Horizon Coordination Tasks
sections.summary: Built on ManiSkill3, the RoboPoly benchmark features seven long-horizon manipulation tasks that necessitate distributed control and tight physical collaboration. Each robot operates with its own wrist camera and local policy to solve challenges like handovers and co-manipulation.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Task Design for Multi-Robot Coordination
Conventional bimanual benchmarks (such as RoboTwin) often assume centralized control of both arms by a single agent, lacking setups that require explicit distributed coordination between separate robots. To fill this gap, the authors developed "RoboPoly" using two 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda arms facing each other across a table. The seven included tasks (Food Serve, Prepare Snack, Clean Table, Cook Pot, Put Object Cabinet, Hang Bag, and Exchange Bread) are deliberately designed so that workspace limits and physical obstacles make single-arm execution impossible or highly inefficient.

### 3.2 Observation, Action, and Robot Setup
The camera setup faithfully mimics real-world distributed systems. A global camera ($512\times 384$) capturing the entire workspace from a side view is shared by both robots, but the wrist camera ($128\times 128$) mounted on each arm is accessible only locally. Consequently, each robot cannot directly see the partner's fine-grained grasp state and must infer it through communication and the global camera. Object starting poses are randomized across episodes.

### 3.3 Dataset Generation
Successful trajectories for each task were generated using the ManiSkill3 motion planning pipeline. Tasks were decomposed into key states such as grasping, moving, and releasing, and smooth trajectories were computed automatically. Each trajectory is annotated with high-level task instructions and stage-wise low-level command texts, providing a public dataset of 50 demonstrated episodes (segmented into 100 trajectory segments).

captions.F5: The seven manipulation tasks in RoboPoly. These tasks require close physical coordination, including bread handovers, hanging a bag on a hook, and cooperatively transporting a heavy pot in sync.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Superior Coordination Powered by Communication and Language Reasoning
sections.summary: Evaluated across seven RoboPoly tasks and eight RoboTwin tasks, DuoMind significantly outperformed standalone VLA baselines. Ablation experiments disabling communication led to coordination breakdowns, validating the necessity of message sharing.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
For the low-level action model, $\pi_{0.5}$ was adopted and fine-tuned using LoRA (a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method). The high-level orchestrator employed Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, a lightweight model offering strong visual reasoning capabilities. As baselines, standalone $\pi_{0.5}$ and $\pi_0$ policies directly driven by high-level task instructions were trained and evaluated under identical conditions. Success rates were measured over 400 rollouts per task.

### 4.2 Main Results
On RoboPoly, DuoMind (powered by $\pi_{0.5}$) achieved an average success rate of 35.8% across all tasks, outperforming standalone $\pi_{0.5}$ at 21.7% by a substantial +14.1 percentage points (and improving from 51.8% to 55.2% on RoboTwin). In complex, long-horizon tasks, relying solely on global instructions leaves robots unsure of who should act next, leading to deadlocks and collisions. DuoMind's VLM dynamically breaks tasks down into appropriate low-level instructions based on visual feedback, facilitating straightforward recovery from unexpected states.

### 4.3 Ablation on Inter-Robot Communication
To verify the impact of communication, an ablation was conducted where message sharing between robots was disabled. Without communication, the average success rate plummeted from 35.8% to 26.25%. The effect was especially pronounced in "Cook Pot," where robots must lift a pot from both sides: without communication, one arm frequently lifted before the other established a grasp, causing the success rate to collapse to 1.0%, whereas communication enabled a 39.25% success rate. Knowing peer intentions dramatically improves timing and workspace deconfliction.

### 4.4 Compatibility Across Action Models
The authors also tested swapping the low-level action model from $\pi_{0.5}$ to the previous-generation $\pi_0$. Across three key tasks, the standalone $\pi_0$ achieved an average success rate of 11.08%, which improved to 17.50% when deployed within DuoMind. While stronger VLAs naturally enhance execution stability, high-level language orchestration provides consistent performance gains regardless of the underlying model generation.

sections.heading: How DuoMind Differs from Prior Work: Combining Pretrained Models with Physical Control
sections.summary: Prior multi-agent reinforcement learning relied on latent communication and joint training, while recent LLM-based systems were confined to discrete symbolic skill execution. DuoMind uniquely couples the interpretability of natural language communication with continuous physical control via foundation VLAs.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Learning-Based Multi-Agent Coordination
Classical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has extensively investigated value-decomposition networks and latent-space communication vectors. However, these methods require task-specific joint training, produce black-box representations that are difficult to interpret, and cannot easily integrate with pretrained robot foundation models. DuoMind leverages explicit natural language messaging, ensuring high interpretability and straightforward compatibility with human-robot collaboration.

### 5.2 Robot Learning and Multi-Robot Planning
Multi-robot planning frameworks using LLMs and VLMs have emerged rapidly, but most remain limited to discrete planning that triggers predefined mobile skills, waypoints, or external motion planners. In contrast, DuoMind connects high-level distributed reasoning directly to VLAs that output continuous joint torques or end-effector actions from images, uniquely supporting closed-loop physical interactions.

### 5.3 Benchmarks for Robot Learning
Widely used benchmarks such as RLBench and CALVIN primarily target single-robot settings. Recent collaborative benchmarks have concentrated on high-level task allocation or symbolic actions, leaving a shortage of environments to evaluate fine-grained, closed-loop physical handovers under distributed observations. RoboPoly fills this critical void.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: By bridging VLM language reasoning with VLA motor control, DuoMind advances distributed multi-robot coordination. Its flexible architecture readily absorbs future foundation model progress, paving the way for real-robot deployments and scaling to larger multi-robot teams.
sections.details:
This paper introduced DuoMind, a hierarchical framework enabling distributed multi-robot coordination through semantic communication, alongside RoboPoly, a new benchmark tailored for long-horizon distributed manipulation tasks.

Experimental results validated that dividing responsibilities—where high-level VLMs handle task decomposition and intent sharing while low-level VLAs focus on fine-grained execution—is remarkably effective for multi-robot control under partial observability. Furthermore, standardizing interfaces on natural language makes it possible to plug and play future, more powerful VLMs and VLAs to elevate performance without re-architecting the framework.

While this work focused primarily on two-agent simulated environments, the approach provides a natural pathway toward heterogeneous robot coordination and human-robot collaboration, representing an important milestone for future multi-robot research.

takeaways: Pretrained single-robot VLA models can be directly repurposed for distributed multi-robot coordination when a high-level VLM orchestrator breaks tasks into short-horizon natural language subgoals.

Under partial observability, explicitly exchanging natural language messages covering intentions, subgoals, and environment beliefs reduces collisions and deadlocks far more effectively than relying solely on visual observations.
Using natural language as the inter-module and inter-agent interface allows low-level VLAs or high-level VLMs to be swapped and upgraded seamlessly without retraining the entire framework.
limitations: Evaluations are limited to simulated two-robot setups (ManiSkill3 and RoboTwin); real-world deployment subject to physical communication latency and sensor noise remains future work.
The current implementation is restricted to two agents due to computational overhead and task complexity; scalability to larger fleets of three or more robots has not yet been demonstrated.
To prevent VLM reasoning failures and hallucinations, the framework partially relies on restricting generated low-level instructions to a predefined list of allowed actions.
